Support Vector Classification (SVC): Maximizes the margin (distance) between the decision boundary and the nearest data points (support vectors).
Logistic Regression: Maximizes the likelihood of the training data.

Support Vector Classification (SVC): Can be linear or non-linear using the kernel trick.
Logistic Regression: Linear decision boundary (can handle non-linearity through feature engineering, but it's not inherent to the algorithm).

Support Vector Classification (SVC): More robust to outliers because it only focuses on the data points closest to the margin (support vectors).
Logistic Regression: Can be sensitive to outliers because all data points influence the optimal decision boundary.

Support Vector Classification (SVC): By default, outputs a hard class label (-1 or 1). Requires additional processing to output probabilities.
Logistic Regression: Naturally outputs a probability score between 0 and 1 via the sigmoid function.

Support Vector Classification (SVC): Less interpretable, especially with non-linear kernels, as it's hard to understand the effect of individual features on the classification.
Logistic Regression: Highly interpretable, as the coefficients directly indicate the change in log-odds associated with a unit change in each feature.

Support Vector Classification (SVC): Best for complex, non-linear data and high-dimensional feature spaces (e.g., text and image classification). Works well on smaller datasets.
Logistic Regression: Good for linearly separable data, large datasets, and when model interpretability and probability estimates are important (e.g., credit scoring, medical diagnosis).

Support Vector Classification (SVC): Computationally more expensive and scales less efficiently with large datasets (training time can be quadratic or cubic in the number of training samples).
Logistic Regression: Computationally efficient and scales well to large datasets, with training time typically scaling linearly with the number of samples.

Support Vector Classification (SVC): More complex to tune, with multiple hyperparameters like C, kernel, gamma, etc..
Logistic Regression: Simpler to tune, with the regularization parameter C being the main hyperparameter.
